items.topic: Just culture — system issues + accountability; blame-free reporting of human error/near misses; zero tolerance for reckless behaviour
items.stem: A nurse nearly administers the wrong medication but catches the error before giving it. Which response best reflects a just culture of safety?

options.text: Report the near miss so system factors can be reviewed; human error is addressed without blame, while reckless violations remain unacceptable
Hide the near miss because no patient was harmed and reporting would only create punishment
Punish every near miss the same as intentional reckless harm, regardless of system design
Tell the nurse never to speak of it so the unit's quality scores stay high

rationales.A: Correct. AHRQ: just culture addresses systems issues that lead to unsafe acts while maintaining accountability; human error vs at-risk vs reckless. OpenStax: just culture is nonpunitive for errors/near misses with clear lines for reckless behaviour; reporting improves safety.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Near misses should be reported for learning; silence blocks safety improvement.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Just culture is not blanket punishment; response depends on behaviour type, not only outcome severity.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Suppressing reports undermines a culture of safety.

items.topic: NGN matrix — just culture reporting and accountability indicated vs not
items.stem: For a unit implementing a just culture of safety, indicate whether each action is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Report near misses even when the patient was not harmed
Review system factors (communication, workload, design) that contributed to an error
Hide slips and near misses so individuals avoid all scrutiny
Apply zero tolerance and appropriate accountability for reckless disregard of required safety steps
Punish every human slip the same way as intentional reckless harm, ignoring system design

rationales.R1: Indicated. Near-miss reporting supports learning and prevents future harm.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Just culture focuses on systems issues that lead to unsafe behaviours.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. Concealment blocks safety culture.
rationales.R4: Indicated. Reckless behaviour (e.g., refusing required safety steps) warrants accountability.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Response should match behaviour type (human error vs reckless), not treat all the same.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Code of Conduct — Quality Assurance Program participation and continuing competence (Ontario).
items.topic: CNO Code — participate in Quality Assurance; continuous learning; self-reflect on competence
items.stem: An Ontario nurse asks what the Code of Conduct expects regarding continuing competence. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Self-reflect to identify learning needs, engage in continuous learning, and participate in CNO's Quality Assurance Program
Competence is fixed at graduation; no further learning or QA participation is expected
Only nurse managers must participate in Quality Assurance; staff nurses are exempt
Nurses should avoid documenting QA activities so CNO cannot review learning records

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Code 6.9–6.10: self-reflect, identify learning needs, continuous learning; participate in and keep records of CNO Quality Assurance Program (continuing competence).
rationales.B: Incorrect. Continuing competence and continuous learning are required.
rationales.C: Incorrect. All nurses are accountable to the Code, including QA participation.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Nurses keep records of QA participation; avoiding records undermines accountability.

sources.title: Code of Conduct
sources.evidence: Nurses self-reflect, identify learning needs, engage in continuous learning; participate in and keep records of CNO's Quality Assurance Program (mandated continuing competence).

sources.title: 9.1 Safety: Individual and Environmental
sources.evidence: Safety culture includes learning from events and improving practice; nurses engage in safety competencies and improvement—aligns with ongoing competence development.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Code of Conduct accountability and reporting expectations.
items.topic: NGN cloze — CNO accountability: report errors/unsafe behaviour; learn from errors; QA participation
items.stem: Complete the teaching points about Ontario nursing accountability under the CNO Code of Conduct.

ngn.template: Nurses take accountability for their errors and {B1}. Nurses report any error, unsafe behaviour, unethical conduct, or system issue to {B2}. Nurses participate in CNO's {B3} to support continuing competence.

B1.text: blame only the newest graduate on the team
delete the chart so no one can review the event

B2.text: relevant persons/authorities per legal and organizational requirements
no one, because reporting is optional forever

rationales.B1a: Correct. CNO Code 6.3: take accountability for errors and learn from them.
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Hiding errors blocks learning and accountability.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Scapegoating is not accountable practice.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Tampering with records is misconduct and unsafe.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Code 6.4: report to relevant persons/authorities per requirements.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Social media is not an appropriate reporting channel for PHI/events.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Reporting errors/unsafe issues is required.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Neighbours are not the required reporting pathway.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Code 6.10: participate in CNO's Quality Assurance Program.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Not a CNO competence requirement.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Gossip forums are not QA.

sources.title: Code of Conduct
sources.evidence: Accountability for errors and learning; report errors/unsafe/unethical/system issues; participate in QA Program.

items.jurisdiction_note: PHIPA / CNO Confidentiality and Privacy — breach complaints pathway.
items.topic: Ontario PHIPA — clients may complain to organization contact person or Information and Privacy Commissioner about privacy breaches
items.stem: A client believes a nurse shared their personal health information without authorization. Under Ontario privacy expectations, which teaching is correct?

options.text: The client can complain to the organization's contact person (information officer) or to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario about a PHIPA breach
Clients have no pathway to complain about privacy breaches in Ontario
The only option is to post the allegation on a public social media page instead of using formal complaint routes
Privacy complaints may only be filed with a foreign court, never with Ontario's Commissioner

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Privacy: clients can complain to an organization's contact person or the Information and Privacy Commissioner about PHIPA breaches. CTCMPAO PHIPA guide: contact person handles privacy complaints; breach protocols and IPC oversight.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Formal complaint pathways exist under PHIPA.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Formal organizational/IPC routes protect privacy; public posting risks further disclosure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Ontario's IPC is the provincial privacy oversight body for PHIPA matters.

items.jurisdiction_note: Ontario/Canada health care hand hygiene — PHO '4 Moments' (aligned with WHO 5 Moments framework).
items.topic: Ontario/Canada 4 Moments for Hand Hygiene — before patient/environment contact, before aseptic, after body fluid risk, after patient/environment contact
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: Which set correctly lists Ontario/Canada's 4 Moments for Hand Hygiene in health care?

options.text: BEFORE initial patient/patient environment contact; BEFORE aseptic procedure; AFTER body fluid exposure risk; AFTER patient/patient environment contact
Only after leaving the building at the end of the shift
Only before lunch and never at the point of care
Only after documenting in the chart, never before aseptic procedures

rationales.A: Correct. PHO Best Practices: the 4 Moments are before initial patient/environment contact, before aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, and after patient/environment contact. CDC clinical HH: clean hands before/after touching a patient and after touching surroundings.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Moments occur at point of care throughout the encounter.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Hand hygiene is required at clinical moments, not only meal breaks.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Before aseptic procedures is an essential moment.

items.topic: Sharps safety — never recap used needles; immediate sharps container disposal; needlestick: wash, report, seek care
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick after giving an injection. Which immediate actions are correct?

options.text: Do not recap used needles; dispose sharps in a marked container; after a stick, wash/flood the area, report immediately to the employer, and seek prompt medical attention
Recap the used needle with two hands, then throw it in the regular trash
Ignore the stick if bleeding is light and never report it
Force the needle deep into an overfilled sharps box using bare fingers

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: never recap used needles; dispose in marked sharps container; if needlestick occurs, report immediately and follow facility protocols. OSHA: flood/clean exposed area, report immediately, seek immediate medical attention.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Never recap used needles; never discard sharps in regular trash.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Reporting and medical follow-up are required after exposure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Never force sharps or reach into the container.

sources.title: 10.4 Infection Control and Patient Safety
sources.section: QSEN: Disposing Sharps Safely / Improving Sharps Safety
sources.evidence: Do not throw sharps in trash; never recap used needles; never force/reach into container; if needlestick occurs, report immediately and follow protocols.

sources.section: What to do if you are stuck by a needle

items.topic: Rapid-acting insulin (lispro/aspart/glulisine) — give with meals; onset ~15 min; monitor hypoglycemia at peak
items.stem: The nurse teaches a client newly prescribed insulin lispro. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Take rapid-acting insulin about 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after; it works quickly and hypoglycemia risk rises around peak action
Take lispro once weekly only, with no relation to meals
Rapid-acting insulin has no onset for 12 hours, so meals are irrelevant
Mix insulin glargine into every lispro dose in the same syringe at home without checking instructions

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: rapid-acting (lispro/aspart/glulisine) onset ~15–30 min; take 15 min before or immediately after a meal; peak 1–2 h with hypoglycemia risk. Merck: rapid-acting best used at mealtime for postprandial glucose. ADA: rapid-acting onset ~15 min; bolus covers meals.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Rapid-acting is meal-related (bolus), not a weekly dose.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Onset is minutes, not hours.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Merck: insulin glargine should never be mixed with any other insulin.

sources.title: 28.2 Insulin and Non-Insulin Injectable Diabetes Drugs
sources.evidence: Lispro onset 15–30 min; take 15 min before or immediately after meal; peak 1–2 h; monitor hypoglycemia at peak.

sources.title: Medications for Diabetes Mellitus Treatment
sources.evidence: Rapid-acting best at mealtime for postprandial spikes; glargine should never be mixed with any other insulin.

items.topic: NGN matrix — rapid-acting meal timing and glargine no-mix teaching
items.stem: For a client on basal-bolus insulin (glargine + lispro), indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Inject rapid-acting (lispro) about 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after eating
Watch for hypoglycemia especially around rapid-acting insulin peak
Never mix insulin glargine with any other insulin in the same syringe
Skip all mealtime insulin forever because basal insulin alone covers every carb
Premix glargine and lispro in one home bottle for convenience without manufacturer guidance

rationales.R1: Indicated. Rapid-acting is timed to meals.
rationales.R2: Indicated. Peak action increases hypoglycemia risk.
rationales.R3: Indicated. Glargine must not be mixed with other insulins.
rationales.R4: Not indicated. Bolus/prandial coverage is needed for meals in basal-bolus regimens.
rationales.R5: Not indicated. Do not premix glargine with other insulins.

items.topic: NGN cloze — rapid-acting with meals; glargine not mixed; hypoglycemia at peak
items.stem: Complete the insulin safety teaching for a basal-bolus regimen.

ngn.template: Rapid-acting insulin is given {B1}. Insulin glargine should {B2}. The nurse monitors closely for hypoglycemia especially {B3}.

B1.text: about 15 minutes before a meal or immediately after a meal
once a month only, unrelated to food
only when the client has no food available for 24 hours
exclusively by crushing tablets into juice

B2.text: never be mixed with any other insulin
always be shaken vigorously with NPH in one bottle at home
be mixed with lispro in every home syringe without checking
be discontinued if meals contain any carbohydrate

B3.text: around the peak action of the insulin
only during dental cleanings years later
never, because insulin cannot lower glucose

rationales.B1a: Correct. Rapid-acting insulin is meal-timed (~15 min before or immediately after).
rationales.B1b: Incorrect. Rapid-acting is not a once-monthly unrelated dose.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Meal coverage requires food timing, not prolonged fasting.
rationales.B1d: Incorrect. Insulin is injected (or inhaled formulations), not crushed tablets.
rationales.B2a: Correct. Merck: insulin glargine should never be mixed with any other insulin.
rationales.B2b: Incorrect. Do not mix glargine with NPH in one bottle.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Do not mix glargine with lispro.
rationales.B2d: Incorrect. Basal insulin is not stopped merely because meals contain carbohydrate.
rationales.B3a: Correct. Hypoglycemia risk is highest around peak action.
rationales.B3b: Incorrect. Monitoring is tied to pharmacologic peak, not dental visits.
rationales.B3c: Incorrect. Insulin lowers glucose; hypoglycemia is a key risk.

sources.title: 28.2 Insulin and Non-Insulin Injectable Diabetes Drugs
sources.evidence: Meal timing; monitor for hypoglycemic reaction during peak.

sources.title: Medications for Diabetes Mellitus Treatment
sources.evidence: Insulin glargine should never be mixed with any other insulin.

items.topic: MRI safety screening — report implants/devices; remove ferromagnetic objects; unknown devices assumed unsafe until cleared
items.stem: Before an older adult enters the MRI scanner room, which nursing action is the priority safety teaching/screening step?

options.text: Screen for implants/devices (e.g., pacemaker, aneurysm clips) and remove ferromagnetic objects; do not proceed with unknown devices until MRI safety status is confirmed
Bring steel oxygen tanks and loose keys into the magnet room to save time
Assume all pacemakers are automatically safe without identifying the model
Skip screening because MRI never interacts with metal

rationales.A: Correct. RadiologyInfo: screen for implants; remove metallic belongings; magnet can move ferromagnetic objects/implants; some devices may malfunction. FDA: careful screening; patients with implants should not receive MRI unless device is identified as MR Safe or MR Conditional; unknown status assumed MR Unsafe.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Ferromagnetic objects can become projectiles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Exact device type must be known; many require special conditions or are unsafe.
rationales.D: Incorrect. MRI magnetic fields interact strongly with ferromagnetic materials and some implants.

items.topic: Cataract surgery recovery — protect eye; light activity; avoid heavy lifting/excessive bending; use prescribed drops
items.stem: The nurse teaches an older adult after cataract surgery. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Protect the eye as directed (shield/sunglasses), use prescribed drops, prefer light activity, and avoid heavy lifting and excessive forward bending until cleared
Start heavy weightlifting and vigorous forward bending the evening of surgery to speed healing
Rub the operative eye firmly several times each hour
Stop all prescribed antibiotic/anti-inflammatory eye drops immediately after leaving the OR without orders

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: patch/shield as directed; sunglasses; light activities; check before strenuous activity. Merck: activity may be restricted (bending/heavy lifting prohibited); protective shield; avoid rubbing, heavy lifting, excessive forward bending; use prescribed drops.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Heavy lifting/bending are restricted early after surgery.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Rubbing the eye is contraindicated.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Prescribed drops reduce inflammation/infection risk during healing.

sources.title: Cataract removal
sources.publisher: MedlinePlus / U.S. National Library of Medicine
sources.evidence: Eye patch; eyedrops; sunglasses; light activities best; check with doctor before strenuous activity.

sources.title: Cataract
sources.evidence: Restricted activity (bending/heavy lifting); shield while sleeping; avoid rubbing, heavy lifting, excessive forward bending; steroid/NSAID/antibiotic drops.
